premise: While looking over land maps at home, surveyor Aniela Warwas asks her sister to choose between two holiday rental dates for their shared summer trip.
story:
Aniela Warwas spread land maps across the kitchen table, their contour lines crossing beneath the holiday brochure. As a surveyor, she preferred clear boundaries, but the two rental dates remained boxed in red.

“July 8 or July 22?” she asked.

Her sister leaned over the maps. “Could we look at the houses first?”

Aniela glanced at the clock. “The houses are the same.”

“They have different views.”

“So?”

Her sister traced a road toward the coast. Aniela sighed and tapped her pencil against the table. The sound came in quick, tight beats. Her shoulders had crept upward, and a hot band pressed beneath her collar.

“July 22,” her sister said at last.

Aniela turned a page. “Why?”

“It gives us more time to save.”

“You said July was difficult.”

“I said the first week was difficult.”

Aniela looked at the clock again. The minute hand had barely moved. She gathered the brochures into a crooked stack, then straightened them with unnecessary care.

“Choose one,” she said.

“I just did.”

“Then say it clearly.”

“July 22.”

Aniela wrote the date beside the rental name. Her pencil dug into the paper until the point snapped. She set it down and exhaled through her nose.

“Done,” she said, sliding the maps aside. “I’ll book it tonight.”

premise: While waiting alone at the gate for her train, gaffer Jagrati Tiwari notices a silver wrist watch resting on the empty bench beside her.
story:
Gaffer Jagrati Tiwari sat alone at the gate, one boot tapping beneath the bench. Her train was twelve minutes late. She glanced at the station clock, checked her phone, and let out a long breath through her nose.

On the empty bench beside her lay a silver wrist watch.

She stared at it. “Whose is that?”

No one answered. A porter pushing a cart glanced over, then kept moving. Jagrati leaned back, shoulders tight, and looked at the clock again. Eleven minutes.

She picked up the watch between two fingers. Its face showed a time nearly twenty minutes behind the station clock. She turned it over, searching for an inscription, then sighed when she found none.

“Of course,” she muttered. “One more thing.”

A woman nearby approached. “Did you find something?”

“A watch.” Jagrati held it out. “Lost property?”

The woman shook her head. “Give it to the station office.”

Jagrati looked down the corridor. The office was at the far end. Her train could arrive at any moment. Her jaw pressed tight as she checked the clock once more.

A whistle sounded. She hurried to the ticket clerk, placed the watch on the counter, and gave her name. Then she returned to the gate, rubbing her thumb against her palm.

The train rolled in three minutes later. Jagrati boarded without looking back.

premise: Chartered certified accountant Jacob Thompson sits in the bank waiting room when a customer nearby mentions aloud that the local branch will adjust its wire transfer fees.
story:
Chartered certified accountant Jacob Thompson sat in the bank waiting room with his folder balanced on one knee. His appointment was already twelve minutes late. He checked the clock, exhaled through his nose, and tapped one shoe against the tiled floor.

“Mr. Thompson?” the receptionist called.

He looked up sharply. “Yes?”

“Someone will be with you shortly.”

“You said that before.”

She offered an apologetic smile and turned back to her screen. Jacob glanced at the clock again. His shoulders tightened, and he shifted the folder from hand to hand.

A customer in the next chair ended a phone call and said aloud, “Apparently the local branch will adjust its wire transfer fees next month.”

Jacob’s head turned. “They will?”

“Yes. Lower fees for some transfers, higher for others, I heard.”

“Wonderful,” Jacob said, without looking at him. “Exactly what I needed today.”

The customer studied him, then tucked away his phone. Jacob rubbed his thumb along the folder’s edge and watched a queue number blink above the counter.

“Could you tell me how much longer?” he asked the receptionist.

“Only a few more minutes.”

Jacob gave a short nod. “Fine.”

He sighed again, jaw set, while the clock’s second hand moved one notch at a time. When an adviser finally approached, Jacob stood at once, gathered his papers, and followed, eager to finish the visit.

premise: Counsellor João Guilherme Carvalho sits at his office desk alone, reading an email that postpones his upcoming automatic monthly retirement fund transfer to next month.
story:
Counsellor João Guilherme Carvalho sat alone at his office desk, reading the email for the third time. His automatic monthly retirement fund transfer had been postponed to next month.

He let out a sharp sigh and glanced at the clock. “Next month,” he said, as if the words had personally wasted his afternoon.

The email offered no useful explanation, only a polite notice and a link to general information. João clicked the link, waited for it to load, then closed it before the page appeared.

He shifted in his chair, tapped two fingers against the desk, and checked the clock again. His shoulders felt tight beneath his shirt. Outside, footsteps passed along the corridor, but nobody entered.

He reread the date. The transfer would happen eventually; the message made that clear. Still, he had arranged his accounts around the expected schedule, and now one small administrative change had forced him to revise everything.

“Fine,” he muttered. “Next month.”

He opened his calendar and moved a reminder, then moved it back, dissatisfied with both choices. Another sigh escaped him. The office seemed to contain too much air and too little time.

João shut the email, aligned the papers beside his keyboard, and looked once more at the clock. He wanted the task finished, the account settled, and the afternoon moving on. Instead, he sat waiting for the next appointment, jaw tight.

premise: Community development worker Miguel Salgado stood in the clinic waiting area while an unfamiliar visitor asked them to fill out the sign-in sheet.
story:
Community development worker Miguel Salgado stood in the clinic waiting area while an unfamiliar visitor asked them to fill out the sign-in sheet.

“Name, date, and purpose,” the visitor said, extending a clipboard.

Miguel looked at the clock. The second hand had barely moved since his last glance.

“Which line?”

“The first one.”

He sighed through his nose and took the pen. Around him, plastic chairs scraped, a child coughed, and a printer chirped from behind the reception desk. He pressed the pen harder than necessary, writing each letter in cramped strokes.

“Could you also put your organization?”

Miguel stopped. “Why?”

“It’s required for visitors.”

“I’m not visiting. I work here.”

The visitor checked the sheet. “Everyone signs in.”

Miguel’s jaw tightened. Heat gathered behind his ears. He added the organization, then slid the clipboard back.

“Thank you,” the visitor said. “Someone will call you shortly.”

“I know.”

He shifted his folder from one hand to the other and checked the clock again. Seven minutes had passed. His appointment was already late, and the waiting room seemed designed to stretch every second.

The visitor pointed toward a row of chairs. “You can sit over there.”

“I’ll stand.”

He remained by the desk, foot tapping against the tile, eyes fixed on the hallway. When a nurse finally appeared and called his name, Miguel gave a brief nod and followed, wanting the visit finished.

premise: Insurance account manager Kornelia Hrabia receives a text message from a friend stating that their group flight reservation for the weekend has been confirmed.
story:
Insurance account manager Kornelia Hrabia stared at the spreadsheet on her monitor while her phone buzzed beside the keyboard. She snatched it up, read the text from Marek, and sighed through her nose.

“Group flight reservation confirmed for the weekend,” he had written, followed by three exclamation marks.

At last, one thing settled. Kornelia glanced at the clock. The minute hand seemed fixed in place.

“Great,” she typed.

She returned to the policy file, then checked the message again, as if the confirmation might have changed. Her shoulders stayed high. A coworker approached with a question about a client’s renewal dates.

“Send me the file,” Kornelia said.

“Should I explain the—”

“Send it.”

The coworker stepped away. Kornelia rubbed the bridge of her nose and tapped a finger against the desk. Her inbox filled with new notices. She closed each one without reading the previews, then looked at the clock again.

Marek sent another text: “We’re really going!”

“Understood,” she replied.

She pictured the airport queue, the boarding gate, and everyone discussing plans while she waited for the weekend to begin. The thought made her jaw tighten. She finished the last entry, saved the account, and pushed her chair back.

“Done,” she said, already reaching for her coat.

premise: Building surveyor Wanda Scott reviewed an automated bank alert on her phone showing her current checking account balance while sitting by herself in the office.
story:
Wanda Scott sat alone in the office, one ankle hooked behind the other beneath her desk. As a building surveyor, she had planned to finish her reports before lunch, but the figures kept refusing to line up. She sighed, lifted her phone, and reviewed the automated bank alert showing her current checking account balance.

“Fine,” she said to the empty room.

The number was lower than she expected. She read it twice, then tapped the screen until the alert opened again. Her thumb hovered over the notification while a tight pressure gathered behind her eyes. She glanced at the clock. Only seven minutes had passed.

A printer began feeding pages near the door. Wanda turned her head toward it, lips pressed thin.

“Not now.”

She reached for the report, scanned a paragraph, and lost her place. Another sigh slipped out. The balance remained on her phone, bright and blunt, while rent, supplies, and an overdue invoice assembled themselves in her thoughts.

She locked the screen and set it face down.

The clock showed twelve minutes more. Wanda pushed back her chair, stood, and paced once to the filing cabinet. She returned to the desk, picked up her pen, and wrote three clipped notes in the margin.

“Finish this. Send it. Go.”

Her shoulders stayed raised as she resumed reading, waiting for the office day to end.

premise: Ambulance person Aayush Kaur finished repainting the wooden bench in the garage alongside their coworker.
story:
Aayush Kaur dragged the brush through the final strip of blue paint while their coworker held the bench steady. The garage smelled of varnish and metal, and the clock above the side door clicked toward the end of their shift.

“Nearly done,” the coworker said.

“Good,” Aayush replied.

They glanced at the clock again, then dipped the brush with more paint than necessary. A bead ran down the bench’s leg. Aayush sighed, wiped it with a rag, and checked the clock once more.

“Could you get the underside?” the coworker asked.

Aayush’s shoulders tightened. “Now?”

“It needs one coat.”

“Fine.”

They crouched, knees pressing into the concrete, and painted beneath the seat in quick, narrow strokes. Each scrape of the brush seemed to take too long. Their mouth pulled thin as they shifted around the coworker’s boots.

A siren sounded faintly beyond the garage, but nobody moved toward the ambulance bay. Aayush looked at the clock, then at the drying bench.

“Is that enough?” they asked.

The coworker inspected the wood. “One small patch.”

Aayush shut their eyes for a moment, breathed out through their nose, and covered it. When the last unpainted mark disappeared, they set the brush in the tray and peeled off their gloves.

“Finished,” they said.

Together, they carried the bench to the wall. Aayush washed the blue from their hands and watched the clock until their shift ended.

premise: Horticultural consultant Travis Oneal sat alone in the airport gate area and read a text message about his flight's revised boarding time.
story:
Horticultural consultant Travis Oneal sat alone in the airport gate area, his carry-on tucked against his shoes. He read the text message about his flight’s revised boarding time twice.

“Boarding delayed forty minutes,” he said, his mouth tightening.

He looked at the clock above the charging station. Seven minutes had passed since the message. His thumb tapped the screen, then the armrest. A sigh slipped out, followed by another. Around him, travelers watched videos and chatted, but Travis kept his eyes on the departure board as if staring could make the time move.

He opened a reply to the client waiting at his destination.

“Running late,” he typed.

He considered adding an explanation, deleted it, and sent the two words. His knee bounced beneath his jacket. When a gate agent walked past, Travis lifted his head.

“Any chance the new time is wrong?” he asked.

“The board is current,” she said.

“Of course.”

He checked the clock again. The revised boarding time still seemed impossibly distant. He pictured the unfinished greenhouse inspection, the rental car line, and the bed he wanted before midnight. His shoulders felt stiff from sitting, and a dull pressure gathered behind his eyes.

At last, the announcement began. Travis stood before it finished, pulled his bag upright, and joined the line. He said nothing, only glanced once more at the clock, wishing the remaining steps would pass quickly.

premise: Hydrogeologist 香織 橋本 received an email notification from her cousin regarding the updated security settings on their shared family account.
story:
Hydrogeologist 香織 橋本 was reviewing groundwater-level charts when her phone chimed. An email notification from her cousin announced updated security settings on their shared family account.

She sighed and glanced at the clock. “What now?”

The message required her to confirm a new recovery address, approve a device, and read several paragraphs about sign-in changes. Kaori rubbed the space between her eyebrows and clicked the first link. The page loaded slowly.

Her colleague at the next desk looked over. Kaori noticed and gave a tight shake of her head. “It’s just the family account.”

She entered the requested code, but the site rejected it. Her fingers tapped twice against the desk. “No. Again.”

Another email arrived, this one from her cousin asking whether she had received the notification. Kaori typed, “Yes. Working on it.” She deleted a longer reply and sent those three words instead.

The clock’s second hand crossed the twelve. She glanced at it, then at the unfinished chart beside her. A warm line settled across her shoulders. The recovery address finally saved, and a confirmation screen appeared.

Kaori forwarded a screenshot to her cousin. “Done.”

She closed the browser, returned to the chart, and exhaled through her nose. The account was secured, but the lost minutes would not return.

premise: Advertising copywriter João Gabriel da Costa completed the weekly meal preparation schedule for his sibling.
story:
João Gabriel da Costa sat at the kitchen table with his laptop open, drafting the weekly meal preparation schedule for his sibling. The spreadsheet was already half filled, yet each new request seemed to stretch the task longer.

“More vegetables on Tuesday,” his sibling said.

“Fine,” João replied.

He typed, then sighed through his nose. His foot tapped beneath the table while his eyes flicked to the clock. The cursor blinked beside a row labeled “Thursday dinner,” and he rubbed the bridge of his nose.

“Could Friday be something that keeps well?”

“It can.”

Another click. Another sigh. He pictured the copy deadline waiting in his inbox, untouched, while he rearranged beans, rice, and roasted chicken into neat little boxes. His shoulders tightened each time his sibling leaned over to inspect the screen.

“Does this include portions?”

“Yes.”

“How many?”

João stared at the clock for three full seconds. “Enough for two people.”

His sibling began discussing containers. João pressed his lips together and entered the final notes, his fingers moving faster than necessary. When the last meal had been assigned, he saved the file and pushed the laptop across the table.

“There. The weekly schedule is complete.”

His sibling thanked him. João stood at once, collected his coffee, and glanced toward the hallway, already turning back toward his unfinished work.

premise: Insurance risk surveyor 兵 王 stands at the municipal registry counter when a clerk informs him that the appointment system has been updated to a drop-in queue.
story:
Insurance risk surveyor 兵 王 stood at the municipal registry counter, one hand gripping his folder while the other tapped against his wrist. The clerk scanned his appointment slip and gave him an apologetic smile.

“Your appointment system has been updated,” she said. “It is now a drop-in queue. Please take a number.”

王 stared at her. “Updated?”

“Yes. Your scheduled time no longer applies.”

He drew a slow breath through his nose, then looked at the clock above the service windows. “How long?”

“We cannot say. There are seventeen people ahead of you.”

His mouth tightened. He took the printed ticket and glanced at its number as if it had personally wasted his morning. Behind him, a woman shifted aside to let another visitor pass. 王 stepped away from the counter, shoulders stiff, and checked the clock again.

“I have a survey inspection this afternoon,” he said.

“I understand.”

“Apparently not.”

The clerk lowered her eyes to the next form. 王 folded his slip, unfolded it, and sighed. He considered asking for a supervisor, but the thought promised another queue. Instead, he sat beneath the electronic display, bouncing one knee while numbers advanced at a crawl.

Every few minutes, he checked the time and muttered, “Come on.”

When his number finally appeared, he rose at once, gathered his papers, and returned to the counter, already wishing the transaction would end.

premise: Stefan van Werl-Arnsberg, a systems developer, observes a bank teller complete the processing and filing of his deposit slip at the counter.
story:
Stefan van Werl-Arnsberg stood at the counter while the bank teller finished his deposit. A systems developer, he had already checked the figures twice before handing over the slip. Now he watched every movement: the teller’s fingers counted the notes, stamped the paper, entered numbers into the terminal, and slid the receipt beneath a small glass weight.

“Is that all?” Stefan asked.

“One moment,” the teller said, reaching for a file drawer.

Stefan sighed through his nose and glanced at the clock above the entrance. The second hand seemed to drag. He shifted his weight, folded his arms, then unfolded them when the teller began comparing the slip with the screen.

His jaw tightened. A dull pressure gathered behind his eyes.

The bystander waiting near the brochures looked over as Stefan tapped two fingers against the counter.

“Your account is credited,” the teller said. “I’m filing the original now.”

“Fine,” Stefan replied.

The teller placed the processed slip in a labeled folder, closed the drawer, and returned the receipt. Stefan snatched it up, scanned the amount, and tucked it into his wallet.

“Thank you,” the teller said.

Stefan gave a brief nod. He glanced once more at the clock, exhaled, and stepped away from the counter, finally free to leave.

premise: While managing the tourist information centre, 裕美子 山田 hands a misplaced leather wallet across the counter to a visiting traveler.
story:
裕美子 山田 stood behind the tourist information centre counter, tapping one finger beside the visitor log. The morning queue had thinned, but the clock’s second hand still seemed painfully slow. She sighed and glanced at it again.

A cleaner approached with a leather wallet found beneath a bench. 裕美子 opened it, checked the identification, and wrote down the name. Before she could place it in the lost-property drawer, a visiting traveler hurried through the doors, patting empty pockets.

“My wallet,” he said. “Brown leather. I lost it outside.”

“Description?”

“Several cards. A photograph. My passport card.”

裕美子 held out her hand. “Name?”

He gave it. She compared the identification, then slid the wallet across the counter toward him. “Check it.”

The traveler opened it and counted the cards with shaking fingers. “Everything is here. Thank you so much.”

“Yes,” she said, already looking past him toward the entrance. “Sign here.”

He bent over the form, apologizing for the trouble and explaining that he had been searching for nearly an hour.裕美子’s shoulders tightened. She checked the clock, then drummed her nails twice.

“Signature,” she said.

He finished and offered another apology.裕美子 pointed toward the door. “Tourist maps are on the rack.”

The traveler left with the wallet pressed to his chest.裕美子 exhaled, straightened the forms, and reached for the next inquiry.

premise: Gundolf Häring, a chartered management accountant attending an evening adult-education lecture, is asked by a person sitting in the next row to pass a stack of reference handouts down the aisle.
story:
Gundolf Häring, a chartered management accountant, sat through the evening adult-education lecture with his pen poised above a workbook. The speaker had spent twelve minutes explaining a chart Gundolf had understood before the first sentence ended. He glanced at the clock, sighed, and shifted his stiff shoulders.

A person in the next row turned around with a stack of reference handouts. “Could you pass these down the aisle?”

Gundolf looked at the papers, then at the clock. “Fine.”

He took the stack and extended it to the student behind him. “Pass them on.”

The student paused to count the copies. Gundolf’s fingers tightened around the remaining sheets. “There are enough,” he said shortly.

As the handouts moved from seat to seat, he tapped his pen against the desk and watched the minute hand crawl. His jaw felt tight, and he breathed through his nose, keeping his eyes on the presentation only because the lecturer occasionally glanced his way.

“Thanks,” the person in the next row whispered.

Gundolf gave a small nod. “Yes.”

When the last handout left his reach, he folded his arms and checked the clock again. Twenty-three minutes remained. He pictured the train home, the accountancy files waiting on his kitchen table, and the lecture finally ending. Then he stared at the screen, enduring each slowly spoken sentence until the room was dismissed.

premise: At a university workshop, product designer Justine Rose receives word from the visiting professor that the afternoon presentation schedule has been moved up by thirty minutes.
story:
Justine Rose stood beside the prototype table, one hand pressed over a stack of sketches while the university workshop dragged through its morning discussion. As a product designer, she had expected to spend the afternoon presenting her revised lamp housing, then leave before traffic thickened.

She checked the clock above the projector. Ten minutes had passed. She sighed through her nose.

The visiting professor entered with a folder tucked under one arm. “Justine, a scheduling change. The afternoon presentations will begin thirty minutes earlier.”

She looked at him, then at the clock. “Earlier?”

“Half an hour. We need to finish before the building closes.”

“Fine,” she said. Her fingers tapped the table’s edge. “When?”

“Two-thirty.”

She glanced toward the unfinished display board. “That gives me less time.”

“We can help set up.”

“I’ll manage.” She gathered the sketches into a crooked pile, then straightened them with quick, precise motions. Her shoulders stayed high, and a tight pressure settled behind her eyes. Around her, students began shifting chairs and whispering about the new order.

Justine looked at the clock again. “Can we move on?”

The professor nodded and called for the next speaker. Justine stepped aside, clutching her notes against her ribs, counting the remaining minutes until her presentation—and then the moment she could pack her case and leave.

premise: Jake Wood, a textile designer, receives a request from a colleague asking him to swap his scheduled studio desk with a different workspace for the remainder of the afternoon.
story:
Jake Wood had just aligned a row of blue threads when Mara appeared beside his studio desk.

“Can we swap spaces?” she asked. “Just for the rest of the afternoon. The light in the other room is better for my samples.”

Jake looked at the clock. “Now?”

“Please. I need the north window.”

He sighed through his nose and lifted his ruler from the cutting mat. “Fine.”

Mara began gathering her folders, while Jake watched the minutes slide away. His shoulders felt tight beneath his shirt. He checked the clock again, then shoved fabric rolls into a crate with more force than necessary.

“The spare desk is at the far end,” Mara said.

“I know where it is.”

He carried his patterns across the studio, stopping when a student blocked the aisle. “Move, please.”

At the alternate workspace, a lamp leaned over the table, its cord tangled around a chair leg. Jake pulled it free, dropped his notebook down, and glanced back toward his abandoned desk. The blue threads still waited in neat lines, interrupted before he had finished.

Mara arrived with her folders. “Thanks. I owe you.”

“Sure.”

He sat, uncapped a pencil, and checked the clock again. The afternoon seemed to have thickened around him. He pressed his fingertips against his temple, then began redrawing the pattern, keeping his replies brief whenever Mara spoke. All he wanted was for the remaining hours to pass.

premise: Noa Cervera, an interior and spatial designer, watches a fellow participant in a community pottery workshop finish glazing a shared ceramic centerpiece.
story:
Noa Cervera stood beside the community pottery workshop’s drying rack, arms folded beneath her measuring tape. As an interior and spatial designer, she had spent the afternoon imagining cleaner lines for the shared ceramic centerpiece. Now a fellow participant added a final layer of blue glaze, turning the piece slowly beneath the brush.

“Nearly finished?” Noa asked.

“Just the rim,” the participant said.

Noa sighed through her nose and looked at the wall clock. Seven minutes had passed since her last glance. Her heel tapped against the concrete floor. The glaze caught the fluorescent light, and she watched each careful stroke with a tight jaw.

“Could it wait until the kiln?” she said.

“It needs an even coat.”

“Right.”

She shifted her weight, then checked the clock again. The workshop leader spoke with someone near the sinks, while water dripped steadily from a crooked faucet. Noa’s shoulders crept toward her ears. She rubbed the side of her thumb against a dried fleck of clay and pictured the room empty, the tables wiped, the centerpiece safely shelved, and herself walking home.

The participant lifted the piece for inspection.

“How much longer?” Noa asked.

“Thirty seconds.”

Noa exhaled and stared at the doorway. When the brush finally left the rim, she uncrossed her arms.

“Good,” she said, too quickly. “Let’s put it away.”

premise: Femke Reijers, a gaffer, learns that her community theater rehearsal group has moved tonight's practice location from the primary stage to the prop workshop.
story:
Femke Reijers arrived at the theater with a coil of cable over one shoulder and her lighting notebook under her arm. As the gaffer, she had planned the evening around the primary stage: ladders, circuits, and a clean sightline from the booth. She looked toward that stage, then at the clock.

“Where is everyone?” she asked.

“In the prop workshop,” said Mara, carrying a box of masks. “The rehearsal moved there tonight.”

Femke stared at her. “Moved?”

“Director’s decision. The main floor is needed for scenery repairs.”

Femke sighed through her nose and checked the time again. The workshop lay across the building, crowded with shelves and half-painted doors. She pictured threading cable around stacks of chairs and ducking beneath hanging fabric. Her shoulders tightened.

“Who told me?” she said.

“I thought someone had.”

“Apparently not.”

She set the coil down harder than necessary, then picked it up again. “Fine. Let’s go.”

At the workshop, actors squeezed between crates while the director explained the revised blocking. Femke glanced at the clock above the sink. The minutes seemed to stick there.

“Can we clear that table?” she asked.

“It’s part of the scene.”

“Then move it.”

She climbed a short ladder, attached a lamp to an exposed beam, and tested the switch. The light flickered. Femke closed her eyes briefly.

“Of course,” she muttered. “One more time.”

By the end, the lamps worked, and rehearsal began. Femke packed her tools, already wishing the night finished.

premise: Ranieri Malipiero, a chartered legal executive, is asked by a fellow amateur chess player at a local tournament to decide whether they should pause their casual game to let another pair use the table.
story:
Ranieri Malipiero sat beneath the tournament hall’s buzzing lights, one hand beside his rook and the other tapping the table. He was a chartered legal executive, but tonight he had come only for casual chess. His opponent, Paolo, leaned over the board and whispered, “Should we pause? That pair is waiting for a table.”

Ranieri sighed through his nose and looked at the clock. “How long?”

“Perhaps ten minutes.”

“We’ve nearly finished.”

Paolo glanced toward the two players standing nearby, their boards tucked under their arms. “They need somewhere to play.”

Ranieri’s fingers drummed faster. A tight band pressed across his forehead. He checked the clock again, then the board, then the tournament desk, as though one of them might offer a quicker answer.

“Can we move?” Paolo asked.

“To where?”

“Another table.”

Ranieri pushed back his chair with a scrape. “Fine. Pack it up.”

Paolo began collecting the pieces, carefully returning each to its box. Ranieri watched, lips pressed thin, and gave a short breath when Paolo searched for a missing knight.

“It’s under your score sheet,” Ranieri said.

“Right. Thanks.”

They carried the board aside. The waiting pair took their places at once. Ranieri glanced at the clock, folded his score sheet, and slipped it into his coat. He left the hall before Paolo had finished explaining where they could resume their game.
